text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average fell on profit-taking Friday as investors called time out a day after the blue-chip index eclipsed 7,000 for the first time.

The 30-share Dow fell 33.48 points to 6,988.96 while the broader market ended mixed before the long Presidents Day weekend. The Dow jumped 61 points to a record 7,022.44 on Thursday, capping a three-session rally of 216 points. For the week, it rose 133.16 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,346 to 1,148 on active volume of 484.4 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"We saw a little bit of profit-taking. I don't think there's anything more to read into it," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
As if recent reports hadn't painted a rosy enough picture of the economy, the Labour Department said wholesale prices fell 0.3 percent last month, the first drop since October 1994.

The news stunned economists and triggered a bond market rally that lifted the 30-year Treasury 17/32, which lowered its yield to 6.53 percent from 6.63 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
But stocks did not follow bonds, with equity investors just a bit out of breath after the recent fally and with markets closed Monday for the Presidents Day holiday.

"There's a tendency to take profits once the market reaches a plateau and people are thinking 'Let me get this done today so I can have some peace this weekend'," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities.
With the Dow already at or near year-end targets set by many Wall Street professionals, some strategists predicted prices would soon level off for a time.

"As was the case last year, equity prices have risen substantially during a brief period, about 20 percent since November 1996 and 10 percent since January," Abby Joseph Cohen, Goldman Sachs & Co.'s investment policy committee co-chair, said in a new report.
"We believe equity prices could enter a trading range," Cohen said, warning that "as was the case in 1996, this would be accompanied by notable volatility and rotation of portfolio holdings."
Among individual issues, American Airlines parent AMR Corp. fell 1-1/4 to 81-7/8 as the carrier and its pilots tried to reach agreement on a new contract before a midnight strike deadline.
UNC Inc. rose 2-1/2 to 13-3/8 after announcing it would merge with Greenwich Air Services Inc. in a cash-and-stock deal worth about $320 million. Greenwich Class A shares rose 1-1/8 to 22-3/4.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 3.62 points to 1,367.19.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 3.34 points to 808.48. The American Stock Exchange index was off 1.25 at 594.15.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.94 to 423.48. The average share lost 10 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,737.859, down 19.529 or 0.25 percent.
